cross_language_consistency_note: The rubric is mechanical: apply the 3-year age floor, then count satisfied indicators among Y1-Y6 and read off the level. To keep a level meaning the same thing for all ten, each indicator was reduced to one operational test applied in the same order to every language, and each language was examined under the same two evidence sources the rubric names (E2 official documentation at the frozen docs root, E3 official implementation repository and release history); E1 was used only to confirm the version string of the toolchain under test. Y1: count distinct dated released versions in the official repository's releases/tags or the official download archive; >=10. Y2: compare the version string under test against the project's own versioning scheme; below 1.0 requires an explicit production-stability statement, which was searched for and not found for either sub-1.0 toolchain (Quidra, Zig). Y3: take the earliest dated first-party release artifact and measure to 2026-09-17; >=10 years. Y4: satisfied only by a backward-compatibility guarantee, a documented deprecation policy with a defined window, or a shipped language-version/edition/standard mechanism. Applied uniformly this awarded Y4 to Python (PEP 387), C++ (-std=c++NN), Rust (editions), Go (Go 1 promise), Java (--release/--source), Kotlin (-language-version), Swift (-swift-version), and denied it to TypeScript and Zig, whose toolchains ship no such flag and whose projects publish a breaking-change log rather than a policy. Y5: count releases dated inside 2025-09-17..2026-09-17; >=2. Every language that passed did so on actual dated releases, not only on a schedule document, so the alternative clause never carried an award alone. Y6: satisfied only where an official document names which released versions receive continued maintenance AND the end of that maintenance is determinate (a date, a fixed window, or a rule that fixes it). This awarded Y6 to Python (EOL table), Java (Active/Retired update trains plus LTS), Kotlin (18-month window plus end-of-support table), Go ('until there are two newer major releases') and Rust ('only ... the most recent stable release'), and denied it to C++, Swift and TypeScript, for none of which does any official document name a maintained released version; LLVM's security document makes backport depth explicitly discretionary. Pairwise check of the ten assignments: the five 100s all satisfy the identical six indicators. The two 80s, C++ and Swift, fail the identical single indicator Y6 and are therefore at the same level on the same ground. TypeScript sits one band below them because it fails Y4 in addition to Y6, and Zig two bands below TypeScript because it additionally fails Y2 and Y3. Quidra is the only language where the age floor binds. No two languages with the same satisfied-indicator set received different levels, and no two with different sets received the same level. Quidra was scored under exactly the sources used for the other nine and was not marked down below the criteria: its one satisfied indicator, Y5, is recorded as satisfied even though the floor had already fixed the score at 0. Symmetrically, no mature language's real advantage was discounted as incumbency - age, release count and cadence were scored exactly as the dated first-party evidence shows.
limitations: C++ scope mismatch: the toolchain under test is Apple clang 17.0.0, a downstream Apple distribution, but the frozen official_implementation_repository for C++ is llvm/llvm-project, so Y1/Y3/Y5 were counted against upstream LLVM's release history as scope_rule directs. Apple's own clang release history is published through Xcode release notes, which are not under a frozen docs root; Apple clang's independent release cadence and any Apple-specific support window were therefore not separately verified. No other language has this upstream/vendor split.

Zig official repository substitution: github.com/ziglang/zig is described 'Moved to Codeberg' and its newest release predates the 0.16.0 toolchain under test, so the frozen official_implementation_repository was not official at the evidence cutoff. It was replaced by https://codeberg.org/ziglang/zig, the source repository ziglang.org itself links to, with release dates taken from ziglang.org/download/index.json. Codeberg's releases API returned HTTP 404, so Zig's per-release counts rest on the official download index and the Codeberg tag list rather than on a releases endpoint. Only Zig required this substitution.

Rust Y6 is the single judgement that separates a 100 from an 80 in this metric. Rust publishes no LTS line and no multi-version supported table; the award rests on the official security policy naming the maintained versions ('only ... the most recent stable release and the latest releases in our beta and nightly channels'), whose duration is determinate but implicit rather than stated as a period. A stricter reading requiring an explicit duration would move Rust from 100 to 80, alongside C++ and Swift. Go's Y6 was awarded on the same basis and would be unaffected, since its rule states the duration explicitly.

Kotlin Y6's published 18-month support window is stated for the Kotlin/JVM standard library and applies from 2.4.0, whereas the toolchain under test is 2.3.21; the indicator asks only whether such a documented policy exists, and it does, but the window is not verified as covering the exact version under test.

Negative findings for Y4 and Y6 (TypeScript, Swift, Zig, C++, Quidra) are established by targeted search of the frozen docs roots, the official repository wikis, the shipped --help/--all option surface, and in Swift's case an enumeration of the swift.org top-level navigation. They are well-evidenced absences from the named sources, but no search proves a statement exists nowhere on a large documentation site.

Y3 for Python, Rust, Go, Java, TypeScript, Kotlin and Swift was established from the oldest dated first-party artifact that each project still publishes, not from the historical first release of the language (for example Python 0.9.0 in 1991 or Swift 1.0 in 2014). Every one of these clears 10 years on the published evidence alone, so the distinction does not change any level; it is recorded because Swift's margin is the narrowest at about six months.
Quidra's v0.3.0 was published 2026-09-18, after the 2026-09-17 evidence cutoff, and was excluded from all counts. The toolchain under test is 0.2.0 and the age floor binds regardless.

GitHub release and tag data were retrieved through an authenticated gh CLI session because the unauthenticated API rate limit was exhausted; this affects retrieval only, not the content of the public release records.
